description: I’m a CS student who builds full-stack projects (C++, React, backend APIs) and enjoys algorithms, graph problems and machine learning, and I like turning complex data into decision-making tools that people can use. Join us if you want to build a polished, well-explained NASA project, and we’re looking for teammates with strengths in geospatial or remote-sensing data, 3D or UI design, or science storytelling and pitching.
summary: **Mars Navigator** is an interactive web map for planning a Marswalk in Jezero Crater, built for the NASA Space Apps challenge "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map."
details:
Project name

MarsWalk Atlas

One-line summary

A web map that plans the safest walking route for an astronaut across Jezero Crater, with science stops, slope hazards, elevation, and oxygen use.

Challenge

Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map

Description

Mars Navigator is an interactive map an astronaut could use to plan a Marswalk. The user clicks a start point, optional science stops and an end point near Jezero Crater. The app finds the safest walking route, avoiding ground too steep for a suited astronaut carrying equipment. It shows distance, walking time, steepest slope, a risk score, oxygen use and an elevation profile for the route.

Mission science goal: [one sentence the team agreed on]

What the astronaut sees:

  • A Mars map with layers: imagery, slope hazards, points of interest, [SHARAD radar coverage] and optional HiRISE imagery.
  • 18 points of interest, each with a reason it matters for the science goal and a photo of what to expect on arrival [if the photo panel is working].
  • A route through the chosen stops, with a summary per leg.

Data layers (three kinds, as the challenge suggests):

  • Topographic: a 296 x 281 elevation grid at about 200 m resolution, source: [name of the elevation dataset and how it was resampled].
  • Optical imagery: NASA Mars Trek base map and a partial-coverage HiRISE layer.
  • Geophysical: [SHARAD radar coverage from the NASA PDS, MRO SHARAD Radargram V2.0. This shows where radar data exists, not confirmed ice.]

How it works: We compute the slope of every cell, block cells above the slope limit, and run an A* search (a shortest-path algorithm) over the grid. The slope limit and walking speed are reduced by a load factor to model a suit and equipment.

What is original

The route planner is our own code. It chains legs through science stops and returns per-leg distance, time, slope, risk and oxygen. The map, panels and layers are built around it.

Limitations (stated honestly)

  • The slope limit, walking speed, load factor and oxygen supply are demo assumptions, not mission data. The risk score is a simple heuristic.
  • Only slope blocks routes. Rock fields and boulders are not modelled.
  • [SHARAD results show radar coverage only, not subsurface ice.]
  • The HiRISE layer has partial coverage, so some areas are blank.
  • This is a concept, not flight-certified.

Built with

React, Vite, Leaflet and react-leaflet, Zustand, JavaScript. NASA data: Mars Trek tiles, [elevation source], [MRO SHARAD via NASA PDS].

Links

  • Live demo: https://martian-map-2pjk.vercel.app/
  • Code: https://github.com/maheen8q/Martian-map
  • Demo video: https://youtu.be/DvRAzidT4cg

Team

Maheen, Ayesha, Hafsa, Umayyah, Arbish

Before you submit, make sure the elevation source name and the SHARAD line match what the team actually did, and that everything in the “Limitations” section still holds. If SHARAD isn’t on the map, rewrite its line as “sourced, planned for integration”.
